critique: All seven KEY figures are exactly right, and the memo handles the trickiest analytical trap well: it correctly builds like-for-like on only the seven common calendar days and correctly declares the periods non-comparable. The weak core is the diagnosis — 'UK was the main driver' restates where the growth occurred, not why, and the memo defers the actual cause to recommendation 3, even though the data plainly support a volume-led story (units roughly doubled 10,014 to 20,507 while realised price fell 1.99 to 1.89), a single-day concentration (2 Dec alone accounts for 41% of the gain), 232 new customers adding £22,948 against 170 lapsed customers costing £11,050, and new 23xxx SKUs contributing £17,402 from a zero base. It also omits that cancellation revenue rose 15x (-£26 to -£416) and that 7 December actually fell, and recommendations 1 and 3 lean on analysis/data-capture asks rather than commercial actions.

But the causal story is thin and partly misleading: Australia's entire +34k swing is one customer (12415) going from 2327 to 35693 with only 4 buyers versus 6 the year before, so the flagship recommendation to 'replicate the Australian acquisition playbook' rests on a single-whale artefact rather than an acquisition trend, which is exactly the risk the Head of Sales needed flagged. It also mislabels the retained cohort (72 identified customers, 172254.69 to 191146.35, +11.0%) because 7231.07 of unidentified prior revenue was silently folded into the 'retained' bucket, and it offers no diagnosis of why EIRE and Sweden fell (lost customers vs. fewer/one-off orders).

The diagnosis is also shallow: Netherlands (+32.2k) and EIRE (-16.4k) are each one or two wholesale accounts (customer 14646 alone is 55.4k→76.7k in NL, with only 9 and 3 customers in those markets), so recommending 'replicate the NL/FR formula' and 'check EIRE local competition and pricing' is misdirected — the real story is account retention, which the memo flags (lost repeat revenue) yet never recommends an action for. It also mislabels absent Saturdays as missing data when the file contains no Saturday trading in either year, and never caveats that the like-for-like window drops 2010's peak pre-Christmas fortnight (111k, 27% of the quarter), so the +20.9% is not a full-quarter read.

critique: The core numbers check out against the raw data: product-line filtering, the 113-day like-for-like window (correctly dropping the partial 30 June), +16.8% growth, Australia as the top mover, the 94,129.35 lost-customer revenue and the 2.2% unidentified share all reproduce exactly, and the memo is well structured and within the word limit. But the driver diagnosis stops at country/new-vs-lost counts and misses the decisive fact that one new Australian account (+66,356) and one Dutch account (+37,070) account for essentially the entire net gain, while EIRE's fall is two accounts and Denmark/Sweden losses are single accounts (30,035 and 21,969) — so the recommendation to "increase marketing in Australia/the Netherlands" is mis-targeted versus account-level retention/expansion actions. Trust is also dented by sloppy arithmetic: 41/42 absent days should be 40/41 for 181-day half-years, the stated 27/26 removed days do not reconcile with 113 comparable days, the quoted full-period revenues (577,565.11 / 623,117.64) do not match a product-only KPI sum (583,166.13 / 626,826.98), and KEY revenue_prior/current silently use the like-for-like basis while the text quotes a different figure.

critique: All seven KEY values are exactly reproducible from the raw data (3,796.24 → 4,771.99; 22.4% on 45 common calendar days; UK +817.97; lost-customer 2,223.92; 18.2% unidentified), the exclusion/LFL methodology is correct, and the memo is concise, professional and answers the assignment structurally. But the diagnosis is descriptive rather than a driver: it attributes growth to "the UK" as a geography while missing the actual pattern in the data — April (−158.95) and May (−92.36) both fell, the whole increase came from June (+968.74), and a single 28 June 2011 invoice (customer 16671, 1,121.28) plus one Dutch order account for more than the entire net gain, so the 22.4% is fragile and concentrated in a couple of orders. The body also contains an unsupported claim that new customers contributed 3,351.13 of like-for-like revenue (the data gives 2,587.92 from new identified customers, 618.98 returning, 713.83 guest), and the recommendations are generic ("replicate UK tactics") with no targets, owners or timing; a Head of Sales would act very differently knowing growth rest on one late-June bulk order.

critique: The memo is well organised and most figures tie out, but it silently drops 30 June from both years: the stated prior/current totals (577565.11 / 623117.64) are one day short of the true H1 revenues (583166.13 / 626826.98, +7.5% not +7.9%), so the KEY period values are mislabelled and the reader cannot see why 113 rather than 114 common days were used. The diagnosis stops at country level (Australia up, EIRE/Denmark/Sweden down) without any evidence on what actually drove it — the data show ~94k of prior like-for-like revenue from identified customers who did not return, concentrated in Denmark and Sweden, which is never mentioned in the narrative and is not addressed by any recommendation; the lost_customer_revenue of 92592.74 is also not reproducible from a straightforward definition (~94129). Recommendations are therefore generic ('replicate the Australian playbook', 'fix guest checkout') rather than concrete actions tied to the retention loss, though the writing itself is concise and professional.

critique: Every figure I re-derived from the raw export ties exactly (205,804.48 / 290,825.86, the 50 shared days giving 147,333.44 to 271,205.94 = +84.1%, UK +111,545.86, churn 41,710.20, 25.8% unidentified), so the memo is trustworthy on the numbers and correctly warns that the two windows are incomplete and that unidentified revenue may overstate churn. But it reads like a data appendix rather than an executive answer: the headline like-for-like growth never appears in the prose, the full-period change is never stated, and there is no volume-versus-price decomposition (units +69% vs price/unit +8.8%) or mention that cancellations nearly tripled (about 3.4k to 11.1k), which is material to whether the gain is repeatable. The data-quality section also misdiagnoses the problem: Saturdays are absent in both years (structural, so irrelevant to comparability), yet a third of the recommendations is spent sending IT after them, while the real defect is the unequal truncated export; and the "+20% UK stock" and "recover 6,250" targets are asserted without basis, prioritisation or risk, and the win-back list ignores that some "lost" buyers may be among the unidentified current customers still purchasing.

critique: The like-for-like basis is methodologically wrong: matching days by month-day aligns 2010 Mondays/Sundays with 2011 Fridays/Mondays, so the 'LFL' drops all 2010 Friday revenue (~36.4k) while keeping 2011 Fridays and dropping 2011 Sundays (~22.6k), inflating growth to 24.7% when an apples-to-apples window (Oct 1–Dec 9, same 10 days per weekday, 251,019 vs 290,328) shows ~15.7%. The reconciliation labels are also wrong (the 36,378.12 gap is 2010 Friday sales, not 'absent Saturdays'; the 22,564.05 gap is Sunday sales), and the memo misstates that 2 Oct is missing in 2011, although the headline figures for revenue, lost-customer revenue (71,496.75), unidentified share (25.1%) and top country (UK) do reproduce. The driver split (lost/new/retained) and recommendations are reasonably concrete, but the core growth number is overstated by roughly 9 points and the seasonal missing-peak bias (Dec 10–23 2010 has no 2011 counterpart) deserves more prominent treatment than the day-count housekeeping.

critique: The seven KEY figures and the reconciliation of the 22 like-for-like days all check out against the raw data (137,930.30 / 156,547.03, +17.0%, UK top mover, 33.2% unidentified), and the memo is tight, on-structure and professional. But the diagnosis stops at naming countries: it gives no magnitudes (UK is ~90% of the delta), misses that the entire net gain is volume/mix rather than price (units +31%, average price 1.80 to 1.61), that four new Christmas lines (e.g. 23344, 23313) add ~27k against a ~21k net change, and that ten customers drive 72% of the swing, so the Head of Sales gets no lever to pull. The recommendations are mostly data-ops hygiene plus a vaguely targeted win-back, and it mislabels already-lost revenue as 'at risk'; minor flaws are quoting full-period totals next to a 17.0% like-for-like rate without stating the headline +13.5%, and not noting that the unidentified share actually improved from 38.6% while unidentified revenue stayed flat, which is why the blind-spot caveat is less damaging than implied.

However, the diagnosis stops at geography: the UK accounts for ~97% of the like-for-like change, so saying the UK 'drove' growth is nearly tautological, and the memo never quantifies the real drivers visible in the data (volume +30% to 180,311 units at roughly flat price, and new 2011 Christmas SKUs such as JUMBO BAG 50'S CHRISTMAS and VINTAGE CHRISTMAS lines adding ~£50k with zero prior-year base). The data-problem section and Recommendation 1 are also misdiagnosed: Saturdays are absent in all 62 cases across both years, so this is a structural closed-day pattern that does not distort comparability (whereas the genuine issues are the asymmetric period cut-offs, 23 Dec vs 9 Dec), making 'urgently backfill Saturday transactions' unactionable, and Recommendation 3's win-back list is fine but the unexplained £71.5k churn figure is left unquantified as a share of prior revenue.

critique: Every figure checks out against the raw data (revenue 443,807.87 vs 504,648.52, 64 common days, like-for-like 346,989.99 vs 474,732.66 = +36.8%, lost 61,142.60, unidentified 1.2%, France top at +48,524.54), and the memo's scope, cohort reconciliation and seven KEYs are clean, concise and clearly structured. However, the driver diagnosis is thin: it presents retained spend and France as broad-based growth when the top five accounts account for roughly half the like-for-like increase (the single largest contributor is a Netherlands customer, +30.4k) and France's jump is flattered by a prior-year cancellation distortion, so a Head of Sales would over-generalise the "replicate the French playbook" recommendation. The data-quality section also mislabels the 13 prior-year Saturdays (no trading on Saturdays anywhere in the export) as a coverage gap and asserts "fix export logic" as root cause without evidence, while the three recommendations carry no targets, thresholds or next steps.

critique: The memo is clean, correctly formatted and most headline figures reconcile (revenue totals, 906 prior-year identified customers, 23.15% unidentified, UK as largest absolute mover), but the central diagnosis is materially misleading: the 17.8% like-for-like figure is an artefact of calendar-date alignment that silently drops all 12 prior-year Fridays while dropping only 12 low-volume Sundays from the current year, when both periods actually contain the same 75 trading days starting 4 January and the real comparable change is about +5.5% — so 'periods_comparable = no' and the growth story are both wrong. The decliner list also omits the Netherlands (−£1,888, the largest decline, ahead of Germany and Sweden), and lost_customer_revenue does not reproduce (I get 608 customers / £49,015.86 on the memo's own stated basis rather than 579 / £46,416.89). Recommendations are sensible but generic and rest on the inflated growth reading, so a Head of Sales would be steered toward the wrong message.

The diagnosis, however, is thin: the drivers are asserted without quantification, and the memo misses the single most notable dynamic in the data — unidentified-customer revenue tripling (22.3k to 70.0k, share 15% to 26%) and cancellations tripling (-3.4k to -11.1k) — while never connecting the missing Saturdays to a real bias in the like-for-like: the 50 matched calendar days pair ten prior-year Sundays with ten current-year Fridays, and Fridays average ~3.4k/day versus ~1.6k for Sundays, so 84.1% likely overstates growth. It also fails to quantify what was excluded (22 prior-year days worth 58.5k, 28% of prior revenue, including most of the pre-Christmas peak), and the win-back recommendation rests on shaky ground since the 761 'lapsed' customers (and the 'new buyers') may simply have transacted in the Jan-Sep 2011 blind spot or now check out as guests; recommendations lack owners, targets and sequencing.

critique: All seven KEY figures check out exactly against the data (47664.04 / 41151.44 / no / 94.7 / United Kingdom / 11049.70 / 29.6), and the coverage problem and like-for-like reconciliation are handled transparently and concisely. However, the 'drivers' are a cohort waterfall rather than a diagnosis: it misses that two new-customer invoices on 2 Dec (5549, ~29% of the increase) and one 1500-unit line drive most of the growth, that the LFL window misaligns weekday mix (2011 has two Fridays and no Sunday, 2010 has a Sunday and no Friday), and that 9 Dec 2011 is a half-day cut off at 12:23. The country paragraph is factually wrong on four of five markets (Germany, Netherlands, Portugal and EIRE all fell, not 'gained'/'declined' as stated), the zero-price anecdote is misdescribed (13 lines across invoices 537534, 538877 and 539856 on 7/14/22 Dec), and recommendation 2 ('investigate the surge… sustain the +18000.40 run-rate') treats a concentrated, possibly one-off wholesale spike as a run rate.

Recommendations are directionally reasonable but generic, with speculative benefits (40-60k recovery, 5% lift) and owners assigned to the Director rather than to commercial actions.

The lost-customer revenue figure (94,798.03) also does not reproduce exactly under any reasonable definition I tested (~93.2k vs full period, ~94.8k vs like-for-like), and the recommendations are generic rather than commercially prioritised.

critique: Every figure in the memo reproduces exactly from the raw data (583,166.13 / 626,826.98, 114 like-for-like dates, 16.2%, 94,763.88, 2.2%), the retained/lost/new reconciliation closes to zero, and the comparability caveat plus owner-assigned recommendations make it genuinely usable. But the diagnosis stops one level short: the +65,675.70 Australia swing is one account (12415) going from a single 2,326.74 order to 66,355.63 across eight orders, 93% of the country's current revenue, so recommending to "replicate Australia digital marketing playbooks" misattributes an account ramp-up as a marketing effect, and the memo never flags that four customers now carry ~47% of like-for-like revenue while EIRE's fall and the 94.8k churn loss are similarly concentrated in two or three accounts. Add the unsupported "stock and pricing gaps" hypothesis for EIRE and the arbitrary 30,000/50%-recovery targets, and the recommendations read as plausible but not evidence-led; quantifying account concentration and price/volume/mix effects would have made this a strong memo.

It also omits that gross (pre-cancellation) revenue grew only 27.4% versus 36.8% net because the cancellation rate fell from 9.9% to 2.4% (~23144 of the gain), that average unit price dropped from GBP 2.67 to 1.67, that growth stalled to +6.4% in November after +55%/+60%, and that Greece vanished entirely (-4607.13). The three recommendations are consequently soft: two are 'go validate' or data-team fixes with arbitrary targets rather than concrete commercial actions on the levers that actually moved the number.

critique: The mechanics are strong — all seven KEY lines check out against the raw data (26.8% on 224 shared days, Australia +£97,488, 106 lapsed customers worth £138,657, 1.8% unidentified), periods_comparable=no is right, and the memo is concise, well-structured and gives three concrete recommendations (though prior revenue is £1,592 low at 1,261,277.95 vs 1,262,870.89, which also makes the 12.9% headline 12.7%). The diagnosis, however, is where it fails a Commercial Director: Australia's "near-doubling" is actually 4.3x and almost entirely one account (CustomerID 12415 = £123.6k of £126.7k), the Netherlands jump comes with customer count collapsing from 22 to 8, and Australia's active customers fell from 15 to 9 — so revenue growth here is concentration in a handful of wholesale accounts, not a healthy trend, and the memo never mentions it. It also explains the coverage gaps vacuously ("missing January days and weekday gaps… confirm they are genuine closures") without noticing they are systematic day-of-week artefacts, without quantifying what share of prior revenue the like-for-like cut discards, and without any volume/price or cancellations decomposition of "what drove the change".

But the diagnosis is thin where it matters: 69% of the like-for-like increase comes from two accounts (12415 Australia +97,745; 14646 Netherlands +92,547) and EIRE's -60,999 is largely one account (14156, -47,245), so the memo's country/customer narrative and its 'EIRE country manager' action miss the real, concentration-risk story, and it never notes that total like-for-like units fell ~5% (average unit price +33%), i.e. growth is price/mix, not volume. Most seriously, the 26.8% like-for-like figure is inflated by weekday mismatch in the month-day matching (no Saturday data, irregular Sundays; a weekday-aligned comparison gives roughly +14%), a bias the memo presents as clean, and the KEY revenue_prior/revenue_current lines report the like-for-like subsets (1,021,571.17 / 1,295,804.61) rather than the period KPIs (1,262,870.89 / 1,423,723.20), so a reader of the keys alone is misled about both the level and the size of the change.

critique: The arithmetic is impeccable — dedup volumes (21,782 lines / 373,082.93 in 2010), the 7-day like-for-like window (331,559.91 vs 376,905.48), the customer decomposition (which reconciles exactly to the +45,345.57 change) and most KEYs all verify, and the duplicate-line data problem is correctly identified, quantified and disclosed. But the memo misses the single biggest driver in the data: invoice 581483 / C581484 is an 80,995-unit buy and cancel of £168,469.60 twelve minutes apart, which alone drags like-for-like growth from +64.5% to +13.7% (2011 cancellations are 31% of gross revenue, never mentioned), so the headline '13.7% growth driven by new customers' narrative and the recommendations built on it are materially misleading; the memo also overclaims 'new customer acquisition' (18% of the 424 'new' customers, £41k, bought in December 2010 outside the window), ignores the weekday mismatch (2010's window contains a Sunday, 2011's two Fridays), and its KEY revenue_prior/revenue_current use the 7-day window rather than the period totals it itself computes (690,863.62 / 398,343.25), while the 'raw data would falsely show a 43.2% decline' figure is wrong either way (-42.3% deduplicated, -62.5% raw).

The explanation of the LFL gap as 'Saturday trading shifts' is muddled (the real cause is that the prior period contains 13 Fridays while the current one contains 13 Sundays), and the memo misses the central insight that the £610k lapsed-customer loss (a quarter of prior LFL revenue) was more than offset by growth elsewhere, so the recommendations read as generic rather than targeted.

critique: The memo's central claim is wrong and internally contradictory: the -4.2% "headline" is in fact the like-for-like change (product revenue 7,948,904 → 7,608,662, -4.3%), and the +1.5% like-for-like figure is unsupported — both periods cover 4 Jan–9 Dec with essentially identical trading days (286 vs 285), so the "fewer trading days" explanation is invented, and the only genuine partial-period artifact (2011-12-09 truncated at 12:49 vs a full day in 2010) is never identified. Much of the supporting detail also fails to reconcile with the data: March/April were -15.0%/-20.6% not -11%, October was -5.5% (not double-digit growth) and November +3.1%, lost customers were worth ~£950,014 (not £908,658) and the retained base fell 13.7% (not 9.1%), the unidentified share is 16.7% (not 17.8%), and AOV rose only because of the guest-order mix shift (identified-customer AOV actually fell £371→£366). The retained/lost/new decomposition framework and the three recommendations are sensibly structured, but a Head of Sales would be led to treat a real 4% decline as flat growth.
